lesson.title: Join or Die: Franklin's Forgotten Blueprint for Colonial Union
lesson.summary: At the 1754 Albany Congress, Benjamin Franklin proposed a plan to unite the colonies under a shared council for defense and diplomacy, an idea colonial assemblies and the crown both rejected but that foreshadowed later American union.
lesson.body:
By the early 1750s, tension was building on the edges of British North America. French forces were expanding their presence in the Ohio River Valley, building forts and strengthening ties with Native nations there, and British colonial officials worried both about a potential war with France and about their relationship with the powerful Iroquois Confederacy, also called the Six Nations, whose alliance or neutrality could shape the outcome of any conflict on the frontier. In response, representatives from seven colonies, New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Maryland, met in Albany, New York in the summer of 1754 for what became known as the Albany Congress, officially called to renew relations with the Iroquois but quickly turned toward a bigger question of colonial cooperation.

Benjamin Franklin, representing Pennsylvania, arrived at Albany already convinced that the colonies needed to act together rather than separately, an idea he had been promoting in print. Around this same time Franklin published his famous woodcut cartoon showing a snake cut into pieces, each piece labeled with a colony's initials, above the words Join, or Die, a stark visual argument that disunited colonies were as vulnerable as a severed snake. At Albany, Franklin turned that argument into a concrete proposal known as the Albany Plan of Union.

The plan called for a grand council made up of delegates chosen by each colonial assembly, with representation roughly based on each colony's financial contribution, meeting under a president general appointed and paid by the crown. This combined council and crown appointed executive would have had real power: the authority to raise troops, build forts, manage relations and treaties with Native nations, regulate trade with them, and levy taxes to pay for all of it, functions that touched directly on colonial governance, since it proposed shifting some powers away from individual colonial assemblies toward a shared body drawing colonies like Pennsylvania and New York, both Middle Colonies, together with the New England colonies represented at Albany.

Despite the delegates at Albany approving the plan, it went nowhere. Individual colonial assemblies rejected it because they were unwilling to give up their own power to tax and to control frontier and military policy to a new intercolonial body they would not fully control. The British crown and Parliament, for their own reasons, also declined to approve it, wary of a plan that might let the colonies coordinate too effectively and grow less dependent on London's authority. Not a single colonial legislature ratified the plan, and it quietly died within a year of being proposed.

Even in failure, the Albany Plan of Union mattered. It was the first serious, detailed proposal for uniting the British colonies of North America under a shared government, anticipating debates that would resurface, in different form, when the colonies eventually did unite, first loosely under the Continental Congress and later under the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution. The very conflict that prompted the Albany Congress, the contest with France over the Ohio Valley, would erupt into open war within the year, in the conflict remembered as the French and Indian War, making the Congress's failed search for colonial unity look, in hindsight, like an early and unheeded warning.
